analysis.one_liner: Let workers form unions by signing cards instead of secret elections, with faster contracts and tougher employer penalties.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate labor committee without a hearing or a vote, despite 37 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The Employee Free Choice Act would change how workers form unions. Instead of waiting for a secret-ballot election that employers can campaign against, workers could unionize once a majority signs authorization cards. It would also require employers to start bargaining within 10 days of a union forming, bring in a federal mediator if talks stall after 90 days, and let an arbitrator impose a binding two-year contract if mediation fails. Finally, it would give priority handling to claims that employers fired or threatened workers during organizing drives, and add triple back pay and fines up to $20,000 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to organize unions are the main beneficiaries. Under current law, employers can fire, threaten, or delay workers during organizing campaigns, and even after workers win an election, first contracts often stall for months or years because there is no penalty for refusing to bargain. This bill removes the employer's chance to run an anti-union campaign between card-signing and an election, forces bargaining to begin quickly, and makes violating workers' organizing rights expensive.

how_it_helps.text: A union would be certified as soon as a majority of workers in a unit sign authorization cards, with no election for the employer to contest.

Employers would have to begin bargaining for a first contract within 10 days; if talks fail after 90 days, a federal mediator steps in, and after 30 more days an arbitration panel can impose a binding two-year contract.

Charges that employers fired or threatened workers during organizing drives would get priority investigation, and firings would carry triple damages: back pay plus twice that amount as liquidated damages.
Employers who willfully or repeatedly violate workers' organizing rights would face civil penalties of up to $20,000 per violation, which current law does not provide.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially in industries with low union density, bear the cost. They lose the ability to campaign against unionization before an election, gain a legal obligation to reach a first contract quickly on pain of having one imposed by an arbitrator, and face new fines and triple damages for violating organizing rights. Businesses that bargain in good faith would see little change; those that use delay and intimidation as strategy would see it become costly.

drawbacks.text: Certification by signed cards replaces the secret-ballot election. Critics argue workers could sign cards under peer or union pressure and never get a private vote on whether they actually want the union, and that a card-signed union could lock in representation without majority support at the ballot box.

Binding arbitration of first contracts means a government-appointed panel, not the workers or the employer, can set wages and terms for two years if talks fail. Supporters see this as the price of stopping endless stalling; critics see it as letting a third party write contracts neither side agreed to.
The new fines and triple damages raise the cost of doing business for employers who lose organizing fights, and some of that cost falls on small businesses even when disputes are genuine.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core promise is real: workers' right to organize under current law is slow and weakly enforced, and employers who break the rules face little consequence. The trade-offs are genuine too. Card-check certification removes the private vote, and imposed arbitration contracts can be imperfect. On balance the bill shifts power decisively toward workers and unions at the expense of employers' discretion, which is exactly the fight it was designed to settle.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate labor committee, which never held a hearing or a markup, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the Employee Free Choice Act on November 21, 2003, and it was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
Thirty-seven senators cosponsored the bill: 35 Democrats and 2 Republicans.
The committee took no further action; the bill's complete history contains only the introduction and referral, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who benefit from the current organizing system kept the status quo without ever having to defend it on the floor, since the bill never reached a hearing or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic: 35 of the 37 cosponsors were Democrats, with 2 Republicans, and the Republican-run committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill removes the election period employers use to campaign against unions, forces first contracts on a fixed timeline, and attaches fines and triple damages to firing or threatening organizing workers. Businesses currently relying on delay or intimidation during organizing drives would lose that leverage.

Card-check certification makes organizing dramatically easier by removing the employer's anti-union campaign window, and mandatory bargaining timelines plus binding arbitration help unions win first contracts they often never reach under current law. More members and more contracts translate into union revenue and bargaining power, alongside the wage gains for organized workers.
